did_you_know.text: Did you know? This chapter presents the principle of retribution: the plunderer who has not been plundered and the traitor who has not been betrayed will themselves eventually be plundered and betrayed.
Did you know? The people’s prayer in this chapter asks the LORD for mercy and calls him “our strength every morning”—the source of power and salvation in times of trouble.
Did you know? The enemy’s plunder is described as something gathered in great quantity, like plunder collected after a locust invasion or like turbulent waters.
Did you know? Isaiah presents the fear of the LORD as a treasure, associated with faith, strength, salvation, wisdom, and knowledge.
Did you know? The description of the devastation includes damage to nature and agriculture: Lebanon withers, Sharon becomes like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel shake off their fruit.
Did you know? The word “now” is repeated three times in the chapter—“Now I will arise… now I will be exalted… now I will lift myself up”—to emphasize the time of the LORD’s intervention.
Did you know? The LORD’s enemies are compared to materials that burn easily: the nations will become “heaps of lime,” and thorns will be consumed by fire.

Did you know? The person worthy to stand before the fire is described by his moral conduct: he speaks honestly, rejects oppression and bribes, does not participate in bloodshed, and refuses to look at evil.
Did you know? Jerusalem is portrayed as a sturdy tent that will not be uprooted: its tent pegs will never be removed, and its ropes will never be broken.
Did you know? At the conclusion of the vision, the LORD is presented in three roles of leadership: judge, lawgiver, and king—and he is also the one who will save his people.
